turns.content: Statoliths in plant gravity-sensing cells are dense, starch-rich amyloplasts. Which physical properties make them useful as gravity sensors?
What happens to those statoliths inside a statocyte when a root or shoot changes orientation relative to gravity?
How can their displacement reorganize intracellular trafficking or auxin-transporter localization before the organ bends?
Which growth-regulating small molecule acts downstream, and how does its distribution change across the organ?
How does that redistribution produce differential cell elongation and bend a root or shoot?

Connect statolith sedimentation, transporter relocalization, auxin redistribution, and differential elongation. Why are direct mechanical bending, chloroplast retrograde signaling, and release of surface-bound hormone poorer accounts?
How broadly can this mechanism be generalized when the species, organ, statocyte type, transporter dynamics, timing, and competing pathways are unspecified?
What cell-type, PIN-localization, auxin-reporter, time-course, or mutant evidence would most directly test the proposed chain?
State the main cellular mechanism of statolith-mediated gravitropism.
